# Catalytic Converter Clogged, But with what?

Replacing a catalytic converter costs about $1,500 per unit. Doing both bank 1 and bank 2 on the same vehicle pushes you well past six figures in parts alone. When your old units come back from the shop looking like they've been filled with white powder, it's easy to assume that simply installing fresh hardware solves the problem. But if the root cause remains, the new converters will fail in short order. The white deposits visible through the borescope indicate a specific chemical environment inside the exhaust manifold that is incompatible with standard three-way catalysts.

The failure mode describedâP0420 and P0430 codes indicating catalytic efficiency below threshold combined with internal cloggingâis not typical of normal wear. Normal aging results in thermal degradation where the ceramic honeycomb structure melts or collapses, reducing surface area for conversion. It does not typically result in a buildup of solid particulate matter that looks like white powder or chalk. This specific symptom points toward two primary suspects: severe oil burning (blow-by) or the use of inappropriate additives.

When an engine burns excessive oil, unburned hydrocarbons and ash from the lubrication system enter the exhaust stream. Over time, this ash accumulates on the catalyst substrate. While soot is usually black, high-temperature oxidation inside the hot exhaust can turn these carbonaceous deposits white or gray, resembling limestone or chalk. If the engine oil was of poor quality or if the PCV (Positive Crude Valve) system was failing, allowing crankcase gases to overwhelm the catalytic converter, this accumulation would happen rapidly. The new converters you installed are likely facing the same thermal load and gas composition that killed the old ones.

Another possibility involves aftermarket fuel additives. Some products claim to clean the exhaust system but actually contain phosphorus or zinc compounds, which are catalyst poisons. When these elements coat the platinum, palladium, or rhodium washcoat, they physically block active sites. In some cases, this coating can crystallize into a white residue visible through an o2 sensor port. If you used such additives before the failure, the new units are at risk of immediate poisoning if the fuel source remains contaminated.

To prevent recurrence without relying on unverified cleaning agents, you must diagnose the engine condition first. Before driving the car, check for blue smoke during acceleration and inspect the oil consumption rate over a few hundred miles. A compression test or leak-down test can rule out internal mechanical failures like worn piston rings or valve seals. If the engine is burning oil, replacing the catalytic converter is merely a band-aid; you must fix the internal combustion issue first.

Additionally, verify your fuel quality and avoid additives that list phosphorus or zinc in their ingredients. Stick with high-quality synthetic oils meeting the manufacturer's viscosity and specification requirements (e.g., API SP for gasoline engines). These specifications ensure that the ash content remains low enough not to foul the catalyst prematurely.

If the diagnosis confirms excessive oil consumption, consider installing an external oil cooler if one isn't present, as higher operating temperatures can exacerbate blow-by issues in older engines. For fuel systems, a high-flow fuel filter and ensuring your ECU is running the correct fuel map for the specific load conditions can help minimize unburned hydrocarbons entering the exhaust.

Installing new hardware without addressing these underlying chemical imbalances is an expensive gamble. The white deposits are a clear diagnostic signal that the exhaust gas composition has changed, likely due to oil ash accumulation or additive poisoning. Fixing the engine's internal health and fuel quality before the next drive will protect your $3,000 investment in new catalysts.
